source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"It supports high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis from accumulated unmeasured acids such as ketoacids, but it is not a stand-alone resolution test.","B":"It establishes metabolic alkalosis from excess bicarbonate and shows that the ketone-related acidosis has already resolved.","C":"It proves a primary respiratory acidosis caused by carbon-dioxide retention rather than a metabolic disturbance.","D":"It independently confirms DKA resolution even if ketones or other acid-base abnormalities remain abnormal."}}
source_row.rationale: An increased anion gap supports high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis caused by unmeasured acids such as ketoacids. Option A is correct. It does not indicate alkalosis or prove a respiratory disorder, and current DKA guidance cautions against using the anion gap alone as a resolution criterion.
source_row.source_detail: DKA diagnostic assessment: DKA is characterized by diabetes/hyperglycemia, elevated ketones and metabolic acidosis; direct beta-hydroxybutyrate measurement is preferred when available, and the anion gap should not be used alone as a resolution criterion. 2024 international consensus report, Diabetes Care 47(8):1257-1275; currentness live-rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential: diagnostic/laboratory interpretation, postprocedure monitoring, device management and potential complications. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

source_row.stem: A client with diabetes has hyperglycemia, elevated ketones, metabolic acidosis, and an increased anion gap. How should the nurse interpret the increased anion gap?
